imageDescription: A pale green arched footbridge crosses a pond covered in water lilies, framed by dense foliage.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Claude Monet painted this view of his garden at Giverny in 1899. A pale green Japanese-style footbridge arches over a pond crowded with water lilies, framed by dense foliage. Monet designed the garden himself, diverting a stream to create the pond, and collected Japanese prints that inspired the bridge. For the rest of his life the pond was his main subject; he made about 250 paintings of water lilies. Later, cataracts changed how he saw colour, and his paintings became redder and more abstract. This early version belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

imageDescription: Two large stacks of wheat sit in a field under a soft late-summer light, with hills and trees behind.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Claude Monet painted Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer) in 1890 to 1891, in a field near his house at Giverny. It belongs to a series of about 25 paintings of the same stacks, painted at different times of day and in different seasons and weather. Monet wanted to capture how light and atmosphere change what we see, even with an ordinary subject. The shadows are full of colour rather than grey. When he exhibited fifteen of them in Paris in 1891, most sold within a month, and the series made him wealthy. The Art Institute of Chicago owns six of them.

imageDescription: Friends relax after lunch on a riverside restaurant balcony under a striped awning, drinking, chatting and flirting.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted the Luncheon of the Boating Party in 1880 to 1881. Fourteen friends relax after lunch on the balcony of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant on the Seine at Chatou, west of Paris. They talk, drink and flirt under a striped awning, the scene full of dappled light and warm colour. The woman playing with a little dog at the left is Aline Charigot, who later married Renoir, and the painter Gustave Caillebotte sits at the bottom right. Duncan Phillips bought it in 1923, and it is the centrepiece of the Phillips Collection in Washington.

imageDescription: Young ballerinas in white tutus wait, stretch and chat in a studio as an old ballet master leans on his stick.
credit: Image: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain (CC0)
summary: Edgar Degas painted The Dance Class in 1874. Young ballerinas in white tutus wait, stretch, chat and fidget in a rehearsal room while the elderly ballet master Jules Perrot leans on a tall stick he used to beat time. One dancer performs for an examination while the others look on. Degas was fascinated by the unglamorous moments behind the performance, and dancers fill more than half his work. Though the scene looks spontaneous, he composed it carefully in his studio from models and sketches. The steep, slanting floor pulls us into the room. It belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

imageDescription: Well-dressed Parisians with umbrellas walk across a wet cobbled intersection of new boulevards, split by a tall lamppost.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Gustave Caillebotte painted this large view of a Paris intersection in 1877. Well-dressed people with umbrellas cross the wet cobbles of the Place de Dublin, near the Gare Saint-Lazare, among the wide new boulevards and stone apartment blocks built under Baron Haussmann's rebuilding of the city. A tall lamppost divides the composition in two. The figures at the front are almost life-size, and the precise, cool style differs from his Impressionist friends' looser brushwork. Caillebotte was also their patron, funding exhibitions and leaving his collection to France. The Art Institute of Chicago owns it.

imageDescription: A young mother sits by a cradle draped in sheer white gauze, watching her sleeping baby.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Berthe Morisot painted The Cradle in 1872. Her sister Edma watches over her sleeping baby daughter, Blanche, through a sheer white gauze veil draped over the cradle. The gauze is painted with light, quick strokes, and the mother's gaze and pose create a quiet intimacy. Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionists, and she was the only woman in their first exhibition in 1874, where this painting was shown. She often painted women and children in domestic settings, subjects her male colleagues rarely explored as closely. She married Eugène Manet, Édouard's brother. It hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

imageDescription: A woman in a striped dress washes a small child's feet in a basin, seen from above.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Mary Cassatt painted The Child's Bath in 1893. A woman in a boldly striped dress holds a small child on her lap and washes its feet in a basin, both of them looking down at the water. The high viewpoint, flattened space and strong patterns show the influence of Japanese woodblock prints, which Cassatt had seen in a large exhibition in Paris. An American living in France, she was invited by Degas to exhibit with the Impressionists, and she made mothers and children her central subject. She never married or had children. It belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.

credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Édouard Manet painted A Bar at the Folies-Bergère in 1882, his last major work before his death the following year. A barmaid named Suzon stands behind a marble counter of bottles and oranges at a famous Paris music hall. Behind her, a mirror reflects the glittering, crowded hall and a trapeze artist's green boots, but the reflection doesn't match: her image is shifted to the right and faces a man in a top hat who isn't visible in front. Her detached expression has prompted endless interpretations. It belongs to The Courtauld in London.

imageDescription: Parisians relax in a sunny riverside park, built entirely from tiny dots of colour.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Georges Seurat spent about two years, from 1884 to 1886, painting this scene of Parisians relaxing on an island in the Seine. Couples stroll, a woman walks a monkey on a leash, and people sit by the water in the afternoon sun. The whole canvas is built from tiny dots and dashes of pure colour, a technique called pointillism, meant to blend in the viewer's eye. Seurat made dozens of preparatory studies and later added a painted border of dots. The figures' stiff stillness gives the scene a strange calm. It belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.

imageDescription: Customers sit at a table in the nightclub, with a woman's ghostly green-lit face looming at the right edge.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec painted At the Moulin Rouge in 1892 to 1895. It shows customers around a table in the famous Paris nightclub, where he was a regular. In the background the dancer La Goulue fixes her hair, and Lautrec himself appears, small, walking beside his tall cousin. At the right edge, a woman's face looms, lit an eerie green by the gaslight. At some point a strip containing that face was cut off and later put back. Lautrec's bold cropping and colour owe much to Japanese prints. It belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.

imageDescription: Peasants in work clothes play cards around a table, one smoking a pipe, while another stands watching.
credit: Image: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain (CC0)
summary: Paul Cézanne painted a series of five Card Players in the early 1890s; this version belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Farm workers from his family's estate near Aix-en-Provence sit around a table, absorbed in their game, while another man stands watching. No money is on the table; they seem to play for its own sake. Cézanne built the figures from solid blocks of colour, giving them a monumental stillness. His approach to structure would influence Cubism. In 2011 another version from the series sold to Qatar for about 250 million dollars, then a record.

imageDescription: A dark cypress flames up beside a sleeping village under a swirling night sky of glowing stars and a crescent moon.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889, while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. It is based on the view from his window before dawn, but painted from memory during the day and transformed by imagination. A dark cypress flames up in the foreground, a quiet village sleeps below, and the sky swirls with glowing stars and a crescent moon. The church steeple looks Dutch, perhaps a memory of home. He died the following year. The painting has belonged to the Museum of Modern Art in New York since 1941.
